what_its_for: Erlotinib is a cancer medicine used to treat certain types of non-small cell lung cancer and pancreatic cancer. It works by blocking a protein called EGFR (epidermal growth factor receptor) that some cancer cells need to grow and spread. Your doctor prescribed this medicine because your cancer has a specific change (mutation) that erlotinib can target.
how_to_take: Take erlotinib by mouth as a tablet, once a day. Take it on an empty stomach — at least 1 hour before eating or 2 hours after eating. Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water. Try to take it at the same time every day. If you cannot swallow the tablet whole, you may dissolve it in about 3-4 tablespoons of plain water, stir well, and drink right away. Rinse the glass with more water and drink that too to make sure you get the full dose.
dosing: The usual dose for lung cancer is 150 mg once daily. For pancreatic cancer, the usual dose is 100 mg once daily (taken together with another medicine called gemcitabine). Your doctor may lower your dose if you have side effects. Always take exactly the dose your doctor prescribed — do not change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose and your next scheduled dose is MORE than 12 hours away, take the missed dose as soon as you remember. If your next dose is in LESS than 12 hours, skip the missed dose and just take your next dose at the regular time. Never take two doses at once to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store erlotinib tablets at room temperature, between 59°F and 86°F (15°C to 30°C). Keep the tablets in their original container with the lid tightly closed. Store in a dry place away from heat, light, and moisture — do not store in the bathroom. Keep this medicine out of reach of children and pets. Dispose of any unused or expired tablets safely — ask your pharmacist about a drug take-back program near you.
what_to_avoid: Avoid smoking cigarettes while taking erlotinib — smoking makes the medicine work less well and lowers the amount of drug in your blood. Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice because they can increase the amount of erlotinib in your blood and raise the risk of side effects. Avoid antacids (like Tums or Maalox), proton pump inhibitors (like omeprazole/Prilosec), and H2 blockers (like famotidine/Pepcid) unless your doctor specifically approves them, as they can reduce how well erlotinib is absorbed. Avoid excessive sun exposure and always wear sunscreen (SPF 30 or higher) because this medicine can make your skin more sensitive to the sun. Tell your doctor about ALL medicines, vitamins, and herbal supplements you take before starting erlotinib, as many drugs can interact with it — especially blood thinners, antifungals, antibiotics, and seizure medicines.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: severe or worsening shortness of breath or new cough (could be a serious lung problem called interstitial lung disease); severe or persistent diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, or stomach pain; sudden changes in your vision or eye pain, redness, or tearing; signs of liver problems such as yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice), dark urine, or severe stomach pain; signs of a serious skin reaction such as blistering, peeling, or severe rash with sores in your mouth; unusual bruising or bleeding; coughing up blood; or any signs of a stroke such as sudden numbness, weakness, confusion, or trouble speaking. Also call your doctor if you develop a bad skin rash, acne-like breakouts on your face or chest, or mouth sores that make it hard to eat or drink — these are common but manageable side effects that your doctor can help treat.
when_it_works: Erlotinib does not work overnight. Most people begin to see some benefit within the first few weeks to months of treatment. Your doctor will check how well the medicine is working through scans (like CT scans) usually every 6 to 12 weeks. Keep taking the medicine every day even if you do not feel different right away. Do not stop taking it without talking to your doctor first, even if you feel better or have side effects.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Erlotinib can harm an unborn baby. Women who can become pregnant must use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 1 month after the last dose. Men with female partners who can become pregnant should also use birth control during treatment and for 3 months after the last dose. Do not breastfeed while taking this medicine and for 2 weeks after the last dose. Liver problems: If you have liver disease or your liver is not working well, your doctor may adjust your dose or monitor you more closely. Kidney problems: No dose adjustment is usually needed for mild to moderate kidney problems, but tell your doctor about any kidney issues. Older adults: Older patients generally tolerate erlotinib well, but may need closer monitoring for side effects. Children: Erlotinib is not approved for use in children.
